title: Replacing 12K LoC with a 200 LoC Skill — David Gomes, Cursor

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk is about Cursor, a coding agent IDE, and how its parallel coding workflows were refactored using agent skills and sub-agents. Cursor is an IDE and software-engineering assistant product used by developers. The talk covers building the markdown-based feature, evaluating it with Braintrust and headless CLI, and iterating via RL training and Cursor 3.0 plans. The presentation assumes familiarity with Git work trees, agent skills, sub-agents, and Cursor's command system. This is a recorded conference presentation by David Gomes at AI Engineer. All evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: David Gomes discusses Cursor's refactor of its Git work trees feature from roughly 15,000 lines of code into about 200 lines of Markdown leveraging two existing Cursor primitives: agent skills and sub-agents. Work trees allow separate Git checkouts so multiple agents can work in parallel without interfering. The original implementation required code for creating and managing work trees, scoping agents so they physically could not escape, setup scripts, a judge for best-of-N comparisons, system reminders, and cleanup of orphaned work trees consuming disk space. The new implementation replaces all of this with slash commands—/worktree, /passive (best of N), /apply worktree, and /delete worktree—that function like skills but are server-controlled so prompts can iterate without app updates. Pros include dramatically reduced maintenance, mid-chat work tree switching, multi-repo support, and superior best-of-N judging where the parent agent has full context and can stitch together pieces from different implementations. Cons include the loss of physical isolation—agents can escape since enforcement is prompt-based, described as "vibes-based"—the feature feels slower because users watch the agent create work trees in chat, and reduced discoverability since the old dropdown is gone, requiring users to know to type /worktree. To improve agent discipline, Gomes is building evals using Braintrust and Cursor's headless CLI with two scorers: one checking if the model worked in its work tree, another checking it did not work in the primary checkout. Early results show Haiku deviates more often than Composer and Grok. Cursor is also adding work tree tasks to its RL pipeline for future Composer versions, since Composer 2 had no such training tasks, and is sharing feedback with other labs. System reminders are another planned improvement. Looking ahead, Cursor 3.0's new agentic interface will get a more native, less prompt-based work trees implementation. Cursor is also exploring non-Git parallelization primitives, since Git work trees are slow to create, consume disk space, and only work in Git repos.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the concept of markdown as code
sections.summary: David Gomes introduces the talk about replacing code in the Cursor application with markdown skills, framing markdown as the new code.

sections.title: Recap of Git work trees in Cursor
sections.summary: Explains Git work trees as separate checkouts allowing parallel agent work, demonstrates grids of agents, and introduces best-of-N (best of 10) for comparing models on the same task. Feature shipped around October alongside Cursor 2.0.

sections.title: Complexity of the initial implementation
sections.summary: Details the original implementation's complexity: code for creating/managing work trees, agent scoping and isolation, setup scripts, judging, harness changes, system reminders, and cleanup for disk space management.

sections.title: Deleting 15,000 lines of code
sections.summary: Gomes opened a PR removing the entire feature—around 15,000 lines deleted. The new markdown-based implementation is almost as good and much more lightweight to maintain.

sections.title: Implementing features with Skills and Sub-agents
sections.summary: Two existing Cursor primitives—agent skills and sub-agents—were combined to re-implement both work trees and best-of-N entirely in markdown. Demo of /worktree command creating an isolated work tree.

sections.title: How the new Skills are structured
sections.summary: The work tree skill instructs the model to create work trees, run setup scripts, and stay on the checkout. The best-of-N skill (~40 lines) tells the parent agent to create sub-agents per model, each with its own work tree, then compare results. Cross-platform instructions and aggressive prompting to prevent escape are key considerations.

sections.title: New Slash commands and workflow
sections.summary: Commands /worktree and /passive start agents in isolated work trees and run best-of-N. /apply worktree and /delete worktree manage changes and cleanup. Commands are server-controlled for prompt iteration without app updates. Demo of /passive across five models.

sections.title: Pros of the new implementation
sections.summary: Advantages include less code to maintain, mid-chat work tree switching, multi-repo support, and superior best-of-N judging where the parent agent can stitch together pieces from different model implementations.

sections.title: Cons and user feedback challenges
sections.summary: Cons include prompt-based isolation being "vibes-based" with models potentially forgetting their work tree over long sessions, the feature feeling slower since users watch the agent create work trees in chat, and worse discoverability since the dropdown is gone—users must know to type /worktree. Gomes notes this is an advanced power-user feature and reduced discoverability is acceptable.

sections.title: Future improvements: Evals and RL training
sections.summary: Two improvement paths: evals to find patterns and improve prompts, and RL training. Composer 2 had no RL tasks for work tree environments; Cursor is adding them for future Composer versions and sharing feedback with other labs. Evals use Braintrust and Cursor's headless CLI with two scorers checking work in the work tree and absence of work in the primary checkout. Early results show Haiku deviates more than Composer and Grok. Better system reminders are also planned.

sections.title: What's next for Cursor 3.0 and native work trees
sections.summary: Cursor 3.0's new agentic interface will get a more native, less prompt-based work trees implementation, since parallelization users likely overlap with the agentic UI audience. Skills will continue improving through evals and RL. Cursor is also exploring non-Git parallelization primitives since Git work trees are slow to create, consume disk space, and only work in Git repos.
